planting.note: Set out rooted plugs in spring in well-drained soil; a compact, low-mounding speedwell bred for a long, dense bloom window rather than height.

directions: This diminutive speedwell stays only a few inches tall while spreading into a dense flowering carpet, making it well suited to edging, rock gardens, or the front of a mixed border. It carries an unusually heavy flower count across a long late-spring-into-summer window compared with older low-growing speedwells. Deer and rabbits generally pass it over, and bees work the small spikes readily. Pinch back young plants once established to encourage denser branching and more bloom sites.

planting.note: Set out plugs or divisions in spring in average garden soil; a tall, patented spike speedwell (PP37,598) bred for reduced deadheading.

directions: Jedi Gem sends up tall, slender spikes of light pink flowers well above the basal foliage, giving it more vertical presence than most border speedwells. Its spent flowers drop cleanly on their own, so the planting keeps looking tidy with far less grooming than older spike types need. Bees and butterflies visit the spikes steadily through the bloom season, and established plants need only light monthly feeding. Site it where afternoon air can move through the foliage, since the tall habit is more prone to flopping in still, humid conditions.

planting.note: Set out plugs in spring in well-drained soil; grown primarily for the contrast between its silvery leaves and dark blue flower spikes.

directions: Misty Blues pairs silvery, felted foliage with upright spikes of deep blue flowers, a color combination that reads unusually cool and silvery for a Veronica. The mounded, upright habit holds up well in borders and containers alike, and the plant tolerates dry spells better than most speedwells once roots are established. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies all visit the spikes, while deer tend to leave the aromatic gray leaves alone. Keep soil on the drier side rather than consistently damp, since the silver foliage is prone to rot in soggy conditions.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings/plugs in spring in lean, sharply drained soil; a compact mounding stonecrop grown for its bright yellow star-shaped flowers.

directions: Lemon Sparkle forms a tight, low mound of succulent foliage topped with clusters of small, star-shaped, bright yellow flowers through late spring and summer. Like most sedums it shrugs off drought and poor soil, making it a dependable choice for green roofs, gravel gardens, or the edge of a sunny border. Deer and rabbits rarely bother the fleshy leaves, while bees and butterflies visit the flowers freely. Avoid rich, consistently moist soil, which encourages floppy growth and crown rot in this species.

planting.note: Set out plugs in spring in average, well-drained soil; an upright autumn-blooming stonecrop with dark wine-purple foliage.

directions: Wineberry Delight builds broad, upright clumps of dark, wine-purple foliage that hold their color through the growing season before topping out with domed clusters of light pink flowers opening from rosy buds in late summer and fall. The dense, self-supporting habit makes it useful as a structural accent in a border without the staking that taller border sedums sometimes need. It tolerates heat, drought, and lean soil with ease, and pollinators rely on it as a late-season nectar source. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the center from thinning out.

planting.note: Set out plugs in spring in average garden soil; an upright summer-blooming false sunflower with dark foliage that sets off gold-and-orange flowers.

directions: Sundial is a tall, upright false sunflower whose dark olive-green leaves throw gold-petaled, orange-centered daisies into sharp relief through the heat of summer. The eye zone softens as each flower ages, giving a planting a naturally varied, two-tone look rather than uniform color. It shrugs off heat and short dry spells once rooted, and pollinators visit the open-faced blooms steadily. Site it toward the back of a border where its height can be appreciated, and divide every few years if the clump's center starts to decline.

planting.note: Set out plugs in early spring in humus-rich soil with some shade; an early-blooming, fragrant woodland phlox bred for heavy flower cover on sturdy stems.

directions: Petalscape Blue Velvet opens fragrant, soft blue flowers densely along sturdy stems in very early spring, well ahead of most other perennials in the border. The sturdier stem structure keeps the flower clusters from flopping the way some older woodland phlox selections do after rain. It handles dappled shade well and tolerates brief dry spells once established, making it a good match for a woodland edge or shaded foundation bed. Cut plants back lightly after bloom to keep the mat compact and encourage fresh foliage for the rest of the season.

planting.note: Set out plugs or divisions in spring in average garden soil; part of Darwin's first daylily series, bred as a compact, early- and continuously-flowering landscape plant.

directions: Coral Blaze is a notably compact daylily whose ruffled coral petals carry a picotee edge, a yellow throat, and a contrasting red eye. Unlike many older daylilies that open a single flush, this selection starts blooming early and keeps producing buds over a long stretch of the season, with spent flowers closing cleanly rather than hanging on unattractively. Its low, dense habit works well at the front of a border or in mass landscape plantings where taller daylilies would look out of scale. It shows good resistance to rust and general foliage disease, and established clumps need little beyond an occasional deep watering in extended dry spells.
